q: What is the inference function?
short: prediction = f(input features, trained model): preprocessing plus the fixed model's forward computation; no learning occurs at serving time.
mistakes: Forgetting preprocessing in the serving path.

q: What is training-serving skew and how do you prevent it?
short: Features at inference differ from those used in training (different code, order, scaling, data source), silently degrading predictions. Prevent with one shared, versioned feature library or a feature store, plus skew monitoring.

q: Name four model-serving designs.
short: Library (embedded), service (REST server, replicated), batch processing (scheduled, model moved to data), cached predictions (precompute/memoise).
detail: Choose by latency, freshness, input space.
example: OCR library; iris API; nightly recs; age ratings.
mistakes: Always defaulting to a REST service.

q: Basic vs ramped deployment?
short: Basic updates all nodes at once (downtime, slow rollback, tiny apps only). Ramped replaces nodes one at a time (no downtime, easier rollback, but versions coexist and verification is slow).
mistakes: Incompatible API between versions during ramp.

q: How does blue/green deployment work?
short: Run two identical environments; deploy v2 to the idle one, test it, then switch all traffic; roll back by switching back.

q: What is a canary release?
short: Send the new version to a small subset of users (region, percentage), monitor metrics, and expand gradually or roll back.
mistakes: Too little traffic to detect issues.

q: MLOps vs LLMOps vs AgentOps?
short: MLOps: predictive models, structured data, drift and retraining. LLMOps: foundation models with prompts/RAG, hallucination, token cost. AgentOps: autonomous agents, reasoning traces, tool authorisation, loops, human-in-the-loop.

q: Give operational metrics for LLM applications.
short: Time to first token, tokens per second, cost per request, token usage, latency; plus quality metrics like hallucination rate and helpfulness.

q: What metrics matter for AgentOps?
short: Task success and goal completion, tool-call correctness, end-to-end task latency, retries and recovery, number of human interventions, planning efficiency.

q: What is PSI?
short: Population stability index: Σ (actual − expected) · ln(actual/expected) over bins of a feature, comparing live vs training distributions; > 0.2 typically signals significant drift.

q: Choose a serving design for real-time fraud scoring, a nightly email campaign and a dictionary app.
short: Fraud: replicated low-latency service (with cached features). Email: batch scoring stored in a table. Dictionary: cached predictions for common words with a library or service fallback.
follow: When is embedding as a library best?

q: Blue/green vs canary for an ML model?
short: Blue/green gives instant full rollback and pre-switch testing but exposes everyone at switch time and doubles infrastructure; canary limits exposure and tests real behaviour gradually but needs traffic routing and monitoring. Often combined.
example: Blue/green for infra changes, canary for model changes.
mistakes: Big-bang switch for a risky model.

q: Why must both versions be compatible during a ramped rollout?
short: Old and new pods serve simultaneously, so clients, shared databases, feature schemas and message formats must work with both; otherwise requests fail depending on which pod they hit.
example: New model expecting a new feature column.

q: Implement PSI for a feature.
short: Compute bin edges from training quantiles; compute shares e_i (training) and a_i (live) per bin; clip zeros; return Σ (a_i − e_i) ln(a_i/e_i).

q: Drift is detected but accuracy is stable. Retrain?
short: Not necessarily: covariate drift may not change the decision boundary. Check performance on recent labelled data, slice metrics and business KPIs; retrain if performance drops or drift moves into poorly covered regions.
detail: ex2 shows PSI up, AUC flat.

q: What are the main LLMOps challenges?
short: Prompt versioning and testing, hallucinations, context-window limits, token costs and latency, retrieval quality for RAG, safety and toxicity.
follow: How to test prompts in CI?
mistakes: Editing prompts in production without versioning.

q: What does AgentOps add on top of LLMOps?
short: Monitoring and controlling multi-step execution: reasoning traces, memory, tool authorisation and correctness, infinite-loop detection, retries and recovery, human-in-the-loop approvals, and task-level success metrics.

q: Walk through an end-to-end MLOps loop.
short: Ingest/simulate data → validate → engineer features → train → evaluate and register → deploy with rolling/blue-green/canary → monitor latency, errors, predictions → detect drift (PSI) → retrain and redeploy.

q: Design a progressive delivery pipeline for a model on Kubernetes.
short: Shadow deployment comparing outputs; canary via service mesh or ingress weights; automated analysis of error rate, latency, prediction distribution and business proxies; staged promotion; automatic rollback; registry alias updated on success (e.g. Argo Rollouts/Flagger).

q: How do you serve features consistently online and offline?
short: A feature store with shared definitions, offline (historical, point-in-time correct) and online (low-latency) stores, materialisation jobs, and versioned transformations; validate parity by comparing online and offline values.
mistakes: Leaking future data in training features.

q: How do you reduce LLM serving costs?
short: Cache responses and embeddings, route easy requests to smaller models, compress prompts and limit context, batch requests, quantise models, stream outputs, and monitor cost per request.
mistakes: Sending full documents in every prompt.

q: Design monitoring for a customer-support agent.
short: Trace every step (thoughts, tool calls, results); metrics: resolution rate, escalations to humans, tool-call errors, steps per task, latency, cost; guardrails on refunds; alerts for loops and policy violations; periodic human review of sampled traces.

q: When is blue/green impractical for ML systems?
short: When duplicating the full environment is expensive (many microservices, GPU fleets, large stateful stores) or when data migrations can't be easily reversed; prefer canary or ramped with backward-compatible changes.
mistakes: Irreversible DB migrations at switch time.

q: How do you decide between batch, online and cached serving for an LLM feature?
short: Batch when outputs can be precomputed (product descriptions); cache for repeated prompts (FAQs, semantic cache); online for personalised, interactive requests, with streaming and limits on cost and latency.
detail: Serving designs apply to LLMs too.
